title: Perceived government corruption reaches a record high and is broadly bipartisan, while the government-business gap widens
source_unit: Gallup World Poll U.S. country estimate and party-conditioned comparisons reported September 2, 2026
geography: United States; adults, with comparison to OECD countries

denominator.unit: Gallup World Poll U.S. adult sample; exact country-year respondent count is not disclosed on the article page

government_corruption_widespread.unit: percent saying corruption is widespread in U.S. government

government_corruption_widespread_2025.unit: percent saying corruption is widespread in U.S. government in 2025

government_corruption_widespread_2024.unit: percent saying corruption is widespread in U.S. government in 2024

observations.method: Gallup World Poll repeated country-year measure of perceived corruption; the article compares the U.S. 2026 estimate with prior U.S. readings.
observations.uncertainty: This is a perception measure, not an audit, administrative corruption count, or estimate of exposure to bribery or misconduct. The article page does not give the exact U.S. respondent count or a margin of error.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults overall; party-conditioned estimates are reported in a separate observation.
observations.counterinterpretation: A record-high perception may reflect salient political conflict, changing standards, media attention, or beliefs about institutions rather than a comparable change in actual corruption.

denominator.unit: Gallup World Poll U.S. adult party subgroups; exact conditional respondent counts are not disclosed on the article page

democrats_corruption_widespread.unit: percent of Democrats saying corruption is widespread in government

independents_corruption_widespread.unit: percent of independents saying corruption is widespread in government

republicans_corruption_widespread.unit: percent of Republicans saying corruption is widespread in government

democrats_2024_corruption_widespread.unit: percent of Democrats saying corruption was widespread in 2024

observations.method: Gallup World Poll cross-sectional party comparison, with the article describing changes in party-conditioned perceptions since 2024.
observations.uncertainty: Party identification and perceived corruption are measured at the same time; the estimates do not identify which event, office, policy, or information source produced the judgment.
observations.subgroup: Democrats, independents, and Republicans in the U.S.; the source notes the largest two-year increase among Democrats.
observations.counterinterpretation: Near-partisan convergence can represent shared alarm, but the underlying reasons may differ by party control, ideology, institutional experience, or expectations of government; convergence does not imply shared reform preferences or collective action.

observations.period: 2026; perceived corruption in government versus business

denominator.unit: Gallup World Poll U.S. adult sample; exact respondent count is not disclosed on the article page

government_corruption_widespread.unit: percent saying corruption is widespread in U.S. government

business_corruption_widespread.unit: percent saying corruption is widespread in U.S. business

government_minus_business_gap.unit: percentage-point difference between perceived government and business corruption

observations.method: Gallup World Poll paired perception questions about corruption in government and business in the United States.
observations.uncertainty: The difference is a descriptive gap between two perceptions, not a comparative prevalence or a verified government-versus-business corruption rate. The two answers may be shaped by different examples and standards.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults overall; party and country comparisons are not assumed to apply to this paired gap without their own denominators.
observations.counterinterpretation: The wider government-business gap may signal a distinctive legitimacy problem for public institutions, but it does not show that businesses are trusted, that government use is declining, or that private alternatives are more accountable.

observations.period: 2025 comparison year; perceived government corruption in the U.S. versus OECD median

denominator.unit: Gallup World Poll country estimates; OECD median across member-country estimates, with exact country and respondent counts not disclosed on the article page

us_government_corruption_2025.unit: percent saying corruption is widespread in U.S. government

oecd_median_government_corruption_2025.unit: median percent across OECD countries saying corruption is widespread in their government

us_minus_oecd_median_gap.unit: percentage-point difference between U.S. and OECD median perceptions

observations.method: Gallup World Poll cross-national comparison; the article states that full 2026 data collection was not complete for all countries, so 2025 is the closest comparable OECD year.
observations.uncertainty: The OECD median is a cross-country descriptive comparison with country-specific field timing and contexts; it does not establish why the U.S. differs or whether the U.S. has more actual corruption.
observations.subgroup: U.S. national estimate compared with an OECD country median; not an individual-level subgroup result.
observations.counterinterpretation: The gap may reflect institutional expectations, political language, survey context, or country composition as well as public-sector performance; it does not measure geopolitical reputation, investment, or policy credibility directly.

related_sources.claim: The Democracy for All accountability survey supplies a separate measure of perceived legal accountability and executive power.
Gallup's institutional-confidence series supplies a distinct confidence measure rather than a corruption perception.

boundary: This record identifies a sharp rise and broad partisan convergence in perceived U.S. government corruption, a government-business perception gap, and a U.S.-OECD comparison. It does not establish actual corruption, individual exposure, specific offenders or offices, institutional use or exit, reform preference, collective action, or geopolitical consequences.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Gallup article webpage retrieved and hashed; U.S. 2024–2026 trend, party-conditioned estimates, government-business comparison, OECD comparison year, and perception-versus-behavior boundary cross-checked against the published page.
